data.title: House Democrats demand answers from CDC on Pennsylvania measles deaths
data.description:
House Democrats on the Energy and Commerce Committee are demanding answers from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention regarding the agency’s refusal to accept Pennsylvania’s reporting of two measles deaths, the first in 35 years. 

The committee’s ranking member Frank Pallone, Jr. (D-N.J.) sent a letter to new agency director Erica Schwartz, calling for a briefing on CDC’s measles response, including why it hasn’t counted Pennsylvania’s deaths in its official weekly tally. 

Pallone was joined on the letter by Reps. Diana DeGette (D-Colo), ranking member of the health subcommittee, and Yvette Clarke (D-N.Y.), ranking member of the oversight and investigations subcommittee. 

They are demanding a staff briefing from CDC by Sept. 28. 

The decision to exclude the deaths reportedly came directly from Schwartz, who took charge of the agency this month amid a pledge to operate independently from Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. 

As of Friday, the CDC reported 160 new measles cases in the past week, bringing this year’s total to 3,294. But according to CDC, there have been no deaths.   

On its website, the agency put an asterisk next to the data and noted that the National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) hasn’t recorded any deaths this year where measles was the underlying cause.  

The Pennsylvania health department on Tuesday said it has now confirmed two additional measles-related deaths, bringing the state’s total to four. 

“Your decision to interfere with the inclusion of the first two measles related deaths on CDC’s publicly facing database is consistent with the many other ways that the Trump Administration has degraded tools to prevent disease spread, damaged the partnership between the states and the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), and suppressed information about threats and harm to the public,” the Democrats wrote. 

The third death “underscores the gravity of CDC’s failure to provide consistent, reliable information to the public as the country grapples with a historic return of measles,” the lawmkers wrote.  

Schwartz has not publicly discussed her reasoning for excluding a state’s own reporting, a radical departure from the agency’s normal practice. 

The state’s health department said it provided CDC with the relevant epidemiological data and evaluated the deaths based on CDC’s criteria.

data.title: 'Real Housewives of Salt Lake City' star says show to feature her Capitol Hill advocacy work
data.description:
Capitol Hill could soon be playing a supporting role on “The Real Housewives of Salt Lake City,” after one of its stars, Angie Katsanevas, says she filmed some of her advocacy work in the nation’s capital for the show. 

“We did film some [of the time] that I spent here in D.C. working with the International Franchise Association (IFA),” Katsanevas, known to viewers as Angie K., told ITK this week.

“So yes, we’ll definitely see some of that” on the series’ seventh season, premiering this week on Bravo, she added.

ITK caught up with Katsanevas on Tuesday as she spoke at the IFA’s advocacy summit in Washington to honor its franchisees of the year award recipients. 

The visit marked Katsanevas’s second trip from the Beehive State to the Capitol this year. She advocated for the American Franchise Act — which proponents say would “strengthen the franchise model by providing clear, consistent standards for franchisors under federal labor law” — and testified at a House Small Business Committee hearing focused on franchising in January.

She said that she planned on making a return visit to the Capitol on Tuesday to meet with lawmakers. The conversations might also include “some hair tips and a few spoilers” from this “Real Housewives” season, she quipped. 

Katsanevas, who hosts the “GoDaddy School of Hustle” podcast, said grit is the name of the game in D.C.

“Everyone’s hustling here. They’re hustling to make a difference. They’re hustling to work towards putting this spotlight on the American Franchise Act. They’re hustling to push this bill to the finish line,” Katsanevas said.

When asked her expert assessment of the hair situation among lawmakers at the Capitol, the salon pro suggested that Congress has got their locks on lock.

“Looking fabulous,” Katsanevas, 52, exclaimed.

“Actually, I’m pretty surprised,” she added.

“Growing up, I would have not pictured that there were so many stylish women up here looking fabulous in their dresses and suits with great hair. So, I’m impressed,” Katsanevas said.

“D.C. is pretty progressive,” she said.

data.title: Trump disses 'hostile and conflicted' judge who blocked Kennedy Center renaming
data.description:
President Trump on Tuesday slammed the federal judge who blocked his administration’s latest effort to add his name to the Kennedy Center. 

The president, who has repeatedly criticized judges who rule against his administration, called U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper a “very hostile and conflicted Judge” shortly after the Obama appointee released his opinion in this case. 

“Isn’t that too bad? We have already wasted more than 6 months ‘playing around’ in Court,” the president wrote on Truth Social. “Time is our Enemy! The Board, comprised of some of the most prominent and respected people in our Nation, is meeting again today. It will be interesting to see what happens.”

The president said the iconic performing arts center is “in a virtual state of collapse,” citing the recent damage to the Kennedy Center’s Grand Foyer ceiling after a heavy rain storm in the nation’s capital. 

Cooper ruled Tuesday that the performing arts center’s board could not move forward with these renaming plans until it gets “Congress’s blessing” and found that the board’s August vote approving the addition of Trump’s name likely violated his earlier injunction. 

The federal judge ruled in May that the president’s name must be removed from the building’s facade. Trump’s Justice Department made several unsuccessful attempts to pause this order, and the lettering was ultimately removed in June. 

The Trump administration has exerted pressure to make a series of changes to the Kennedy Center. Last year, the president removed half of the center’s traditionally-bipartisan board, replaced these members with allies to his administration and named himself as the new chair. 

These changes have been opposed by Rep. Joyce Beatty (D-Ohio), an ex officio board member who challenged the Trump administration in a lawsuit. 

“The law is extremely clear: The John F. Kennedy Center is named for President Kennedy — and no one else. But President Trump is holding the Kennedy Center hostage unless he can put his name on this sacred memorial,” Beatty said in a statement following Cooper’s ruling. 

“The Court just rejected this proposal for the second time,” she continued. “This unlawfulness is as breathtaking as it is wrong, and it needs to stop.”

data.title: Blanche dodges question on whether he asked for DiGenova's resignation
data.description:
Attorney General Todd Blanche dodged a question Tuesday about whether he asked for the resignation of Trump-ally Joe diGenova from the Justice Department amid reports that there was a tense phone call between the two before the lawyer’s departure.

“I don’t want to talk about communications I have with prosecutors. It’s not fair to them. It’s not fair to the process,” Blanche told reporters as he led a White House press briefing in the Rose Garden.

“He resigned last week. He came out of retirement to help the president, and to help us and we are very appreciative of the work that he did,” he continued.

DiGenova was tapped in April to lead an investigation into several of President Trump’s perceived enemies. He resigned last week, suggesting he was being asked to move too fast on the cases.

Asked why he resigned, diGenova told The Associated Press: “There’s plenty of evidence in all of these cases to prove the theories of prosecution. It just takes time to get there, and some people want to get there a little faster than others — and you can’t do that.”

In another interview with the New York Post, he said: “If you want indictments where there’s no evidence, you have an ethical problem.”

CNN reported Monday that diGenova resigned a day after a tense phone conversation with Blanche, citing sources familiar.

Blanche noted that diGenova said “some different things to different outlets, which is fine.”

“I very much appreciate the work that he did for us and for the administration,” he said. “Any investigations that he’s working of course continue, like they do, like any investigation does when somebody leaves. And we’re not going to slow down just because somebody leaves.”

Prosecutors on the case have reportedly focused on former CIA Director John Brennan and have also pursued information about those who worked on the Mar-a-Lago classified documents case against the president during the Biden administration.

data.title: Blanche dismisses concerns about Trump Jr's wedding gift from Putin ally
data.description:
Attorney General Todd Blanche dismissed concerns over a wedding gift to Donald Trump Jr. from an ally of Russian President Vladimir Putin earlier this year. 

“The president’s son has said that he’s a very close friend, and that he accepted a gift in the weekend of his wedding,” Blanche told reporters at the White House press briefing when asked if it was appropriate for Trump Jr. to accept the gift and if he would investigate if everything was appropriately reported as a gift. 

“When you say ‘am I investigating?’ Am I investigating what? And when you say this person is a friend of Putin, I don’t even know if that’s true or not,” he continued. “I like that it’s fun to talk about this issue and the rhetoric around it, but I think all of the relevant people involved, the president and his kids have already addressed it.” 

“I don’t have any information. I don’t know this person either,” he said. 

ProPublica reported on Monday that Russian oligarch Umar Kremlev funded Trump Jr. and wife Bettina Anderson’s lavish wedding festivities in the Bahamas, which included a private island and a fireworks show. 

Democrats and critics were quick to lash out at the Trump administration over potential ethics violations and national security concerns. 

Anderson, who is now Bettina Trump, responded to the fallout over the report in an Instagram post defending the wedding. 

“Our friend Umar very generously hosted two incredible nights of celebrations for us AFTER our wedding,” the post read. “It was an extraordinarily generous wedding gift from a friend, and something for which we were and remain incredibly grateful.”

The president did not attend the wedding, but said in a statement to the New York Times that he had “no idea” who Kremlev was and said that the Russian oligarch “didn’t pay for Don and Bettina’s wedding, which took place at a totally different location, and on a different day.”

data.title: How IRS's 2027 tax brackets may change, according to new projections
data.description:
(NEXSTAR) — Inflation may remain top of mind for you, with the latest report showing rates holding steady through August. As pesky as it may be, it may also lead to yet another adjustment in our tax brackets, according to a new prediction.

The IRS typically announces changes that will impact how you file taxes each fall. Potentially the most impactful to most taxpayers is the adjustment to tax brackets.

That announcement came in early October last year, when the IRS released the federal brackets for 2026, which apply to the returns we will file next year.

In a few weeks, the IRS is expected to share what the tax brackets will be for the 2027 filing season. These adjustments are meant to address “bracket creep,” which occurs when your income goes up faster than the tax thresholds built into the IRS code, potentially causing your tax bill to increase. Without a threshold adjustment, inflation could offset wage gain and taxpayers could find themselves paying higher taxes without real income growth.

A report from Bloomberg Tax suggests the IRS could enact a 3.2% increase for 2027 due to inflation, up from the 2.7% increase rolled out last year.

Bloomberg’s report estimates that all seven tiers of the IRS’s tax brackets will see a bump in 2027:

It’s worth noting, though, that these are only projections (Bloomberg Tax’s projections for 2026, however, were in line with the true brackets). The actual updates to tax provisions aren’t expected from the IRS for at least a few more weeks.

If the tax brackets do change as expected, you’ll likely also see a larger paycheck in 2027.

The tax filing deadline in 2027 is April 15.

data.title: Kennedy Center board votes to close main building for renovations
data.description:
The Kennedy Center board voted Tuesday to immediately close the venue’s main building for renovations, according to a source familiar, as the board argues that only President Trump can raise enough money to save it.

The vote comes after officials indicated that the performing arts center faces “certain fiscal collapse within weeks,” with a draft resolution describing the center as on the brink of bankruptcy, soon to be unable to make payroll or routine maintenance contracts. 

The board, handpicked by Trump, has also said the building was “unsafe for continued occupancy,” pointing to a recent water leak that caused a partial collapse of the grand foyer ceiling.

Minutes before the vote was scheduled to take place, U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper again blocked the board’s attempt to add Trump’s name to the facade. It was the second time that the judge found the board’s action was likely unlawful. 

“Simply put, Defendants cannot install memorials for President Trump or anyone or anything else at the Kennedy Center without Congress’s blessing,” Cooper wrote. “The board resolution bucks a federal court order and a statute Congress enacted.”

The resolutions point to Trump’s fundraising skills as the center’s only saving grace. The board of trustees was restructured by the president last February, when he fired half the board and installed 14 new members.

“The Board understands that without such appropriate recognition it is unlikely that President Trump will provide the fundamental oversight of the renovation of the main building and lead the fiscal rescue of the Center,” the resolution stated.

Justice Department attorneys, who are representing the Kennedy Center in the ongoing legal challenge, told Cooper during a hearing last month that the center was in “structural and financial disarray,” arguing further court intervention would impede the renovation project. 

Cooper rejected that notion as “not quite fair,” noting that his initial order in late May allowed “necessary maintenance and repair work” to continue.  

Trump’s name was added to the Kennedy Center earlier this year after a board vote in December 2025. But there was outrage over the addition of the Trump name, and Rep. Joyce Beatty (D-Ohio), an ex officio board member, brought a lawsuit to stop the name change.

The president’s name was stripped from the building in June after a ruling said it violated federal law, but in August, the board voted on a resolution that would re-add Trump’s name in the form of two inscriptions.

data.title: Crypto bill falls short in early hurdle on Senate floor
data.description:
A cryptocurrency regulation bill failed to advance on the Senate floor Tuesday, after all Democrats and a few Republicans blocked a procedural vote. 

The Senate voted 49-50 on a motion to proceed with consideration of the Clarity Act, failing to reach the required 60-vote threshold. It marks a major setback for the industry, which has long pushed for the measure setting up a regulatory framework for the crypto market. 

The vote Tuesday came amid a flurry of last-minute efforts to strike a deal between Republicans and crypto-friendly Democrats.  

About a dozen Democrats were considered potential yes votes. But they ultimately declined to support the legislation after the two sides failed to reach an agreement on ethics rules amid lingering concerns about President Trump and his family’s involvement in the crypto industry. 

Senate Republicans put forward what an aide described as their “last, best and final offer” on Sunday, unveiling updated bill text with changes to the ethics language and a several other sections at the heart of negotiations. 

The new White House-approved ethics provision builds on earlier language that barred public officials, including the president, from issuing or sponsoring crypto assets. 

It initially only gave enforcement power to the Department of Justice (DOJ). But after pushback from Democrats, the latest version also allows state attorneys general to bring cases against the agency or crypto exchanges over violations. 

This still fell short for Democrats. Sen. Raphael Warnock (D-Ga.) suggested Monday that there were “a whole lot of loopholes” in the new ethics language. 

“I will tell you this: Democrats should not advance a bill that does not address the Trump family’s approach to this, where they’re clearly focused on enriching themselves,” he told reporters.

data.title: Talarico leads Paxton by 3 points in new Texas Senate poll
data.description:
Texas Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico (D) is still leading his GOP challenger, state Attorney General Ken Paxton, according to a new poll released Tuesday.

The Telemundo/Mason-Dixon Polling & Research survey found the Democrat, a Texas state representative, held a three-point advantage over his Republican opponent less than two months out before November’s midterms.

Forty-six percent of the Texas voters surveyed supported the state lawmaker, while 43 percent backed the attorney general.

Additionally, three percent of respondents indicated they would vote for Libertarian Party candidate Ted Brown, and the remaining 8 percent said they were still undecided.

Talarico notably posted a strong lead among independent respondents, 51 percent of whom said they would support him over Paxton — who garnered just 30 percent of their backing. Thirteen percent of independents said they had yet to make up their mind about who they would vote for in this race. 

The state representative also had an 18-point advantage among Hispanic voters and 75-point edge with Black voters against his Republican opponent. Among white respondents, Paxton had an 18-point lead.

The Democrat has generally pulled ahead of Paxton after the Texas attorney general beat incumbent Sen. John Cornyn in the state’s GOP primary runoff in May. The Cook Political Report, a nonpartisan election forecaster, shifted its rating for this race from “leans Republican” to a “toss up” after Cornyn’s defeat.

Two June Siena University polls found the two candidates tied, first at 46 and then at 47 percent. By the end of July, Talarico had pulled ahead of Paxton by four percentage points in this polling center’s survey. 

Paxton had a narrow one-point advantage over the Democrat in an Emerson College poll conducted in early August, earning 47 percent of respondents’ support.

Almost a quarter of Texas voters Telemundo surveyed, 24 percent, said economic factors would most motivate how they cast their vote in the midterm races. Other major issues respondents identified were inflation and living costs — amounting for 23 percent of responses — as well as immigration at 18 percent.

Economic concerns have been top of mind for voters across the nation this election cycle, amid surging energy prices during the ongoing Iran war and President Trump’s tariff fight with Canada. 

The Telemundo poll was conducted among a total of 625 registered Texas voters from Sept. 8-10 with an approximately 4 percentage point error margin.

data.title: Dem rep asks Bessent to 'talk sense' into Trump on regulating AI
data.description:
Democratic Rep. Stephen Lynch (Mass.) on Tuesday urged Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to convince President Trump to reverse course on regulating artificial intelligence (AI).

During Bessent’s appearance before the House Financial Services Committee, Lynch said Trump does not have “a grasp” of “what we’re dealing with” regarding AI.

“I’ll be honest, I don’t think the president could spell AI if I gave him the first letter,” quipped the Massachusetts Democrat, the ranking member of a House Financial Services subcommittee focused on AI.

The Commerce Department has worked with leading AI labs on evaluating models before they are deployed, under a voluntary program.

Earlier this summer, the Trump administration briefly held up new models from OpenAI and Anthropic, before allowing the companies to release their GPT 5.6 and Fables and Mythos models, respectively.

Trump has dismissed the need for beefed-up regulations on AI, even as industry leaders argue for reigning in the pace of development. Trump said Monday the only “guardrails” AI needs is a “STRONG AND SMART” president.

The president wrote on Truth Social, “We already have tremendous CRIMINAL and REGULATORY power over these companies!” adding there is a “SICK conspiracy” in the U.S. against AI and data centers.

During Tuesday’s hearing, Lynch credited Bessent with “suggesting some things” on AI “that are thoughtful and … cautionary.” The veteran lawmaker later said “we’ve lost control” of AI, referencing OpenAI recently hacking the systems of Hugging Face, which Nvidia announced it will purchase earlier this month.

“Do you think the president understands that it probably doesn’t matter whether the good guys develop a superintelligence or the bad guys develop a superintelligence?” Lynch remarked. “If you don’t have control of that entity, and it has preferences and goals that are inimical to the existence humanity, it won’t matter.”

Bessent pushed back, saying it “matters a great deal” whether the U.S. or China lead on AI. Lynch then cut the Treasury secretary off, reiterating his view that “the entity itself is what is the danger to us all,” not the possibility of China leading on AI.

“We keep hearing about this race, this race against China. … Well, we don’t control the entity that we’re trying to create, and neither does China,” Lynch said.

“What I’m saying is, I hope there’s a way that you might be able to talk sense to the president about AI and the threat that you and I know it presents,” the Massachusetts lawmaker later told Bessent.

Bessent responded saying Trump was “completely aligned” with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang on AI development. While Huang was speaking at the All-In Summit in Los Angeles on Monday, Trump called him and said concerns about AI were a “hoax.”

“The data centers are great, and they make people wealthy, and they make states wealthy,” the president said after Huang put him on speaker phone, according to a video summit attendee Ben Pouladian shared online.

Earlier this month, Huang urged policymakers to regulate “practical and actual” harms of AI instead of “theoretical and hypothetical” effects.

“We want to make sure that the technology advances in a safe way and … the more advanced it is, the safer and more practical it could be,” Huang told reporters at the G20 Innovation Ministerial in Chapel Hill, N.C.
